content: Anxiety disorders are a group of conditions that can significantly impair functioning and are commonly observed in children and adolescents. Early recognition of these disorders and the success of pharmacological treatments in adults have prompted interest in using medications to treat anxiety disorders in younger populations. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of medications for treating anxiety disorders in children and adolescents. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Depression, Anxiety & Neurosis Group specialized register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PsycINFO, covering studies up to August 2008. Efforts were also made to identify unpublished studies and additional references from retrieved articles. The review included all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated pharmacotherapy for anxiety disorders in this population. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of RCTs for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the quality of the trials. Missing data were sought by contacting study investigators. The analysis stratified results by medication class and specific agents, particularly focusing on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Both dichotomous and continuous outcomes were analyzed using a random-effects model, with assessments of heterogeneity and subgroup or sensitivity analyses performed. The review included 22 short-term RCTs (lasting 16 weeks or less) with a total of 2,519 participants. Most of these trials (15 out of 22) evaluated the efficacy of SSRIs. The response rates to medication and placebo were 58.1% and 31.5%, respectively, based on data from 14 studies, yielding a number needed to treat (NNT) of 4. In a post-hoc analysis, medication was found to be more effective than placebo in reducing overall symptom severity in pediatric obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), with a weighted mean difference (WMD) of -4.45 (95% confidence interval: -5.94 to -2.97) based on data from 7 studies involving 765 participants. While medications were generally more effective than placebo, they were less well tolerated. However, the proportion of participants who discontinued treatment due to drug-related adverse events was relatively low, at 4.9%. The authors concluded that pharmacological treatments can be effective in reducing core symptoms of anxiety disorders in children and adolescents and should be considered as part of the treatment strategy for these conditions. The majority of evidence supporting efficacy comes from studies on SSRIs, particularly in the treatment of pediatric OCD. There is no definitive evidence to suggest that one class of medication is superior in efficacy or tolerability compared to others. Given the limited data available for medications other than SSRIs and venlafaxine, the routine use of benzodiazepines is not recommended due to concerns about dependency and adverse events associated with this drug class. Future research should focus on identifying clinical factors that may influence treatment outcomes, evaluating the long-term efficacy of pharmacological treatments, determining optimal dosages, and conducting direct comparisons between pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy.
